evidence_quotes.quote: This paper provides the taxonomy of country experiences in managing their water utilities. Institutions for water supply for various uses and their financial implications are analysed.

In this section, we develop an empirical model to analyse cross-country determinants of cost recovery levels. In particular, we want to explore the likelihood of efficiency impacts of water ownership arrangements while controlling for other factors.

where CostReci: Cost recovery level in country i. This variable is scalar taking values from 1 to 5 to reflect increasing attempt at recovering costs of water production (CostRec = 1 no attempt to recover costs; Costrec = 2 only part of O&M costs are recovered; CostRec = 3 full O&M costs are recovered; Costrec = 4 charges cover O&M costs and part of capital costs; and Costrec = 5 full cost recovery.

Ownership: Water utility ownership nationwide. The variable takes a value of 1 when more than 75 per cent of water utilities are public. A value of 2 is assigned when government ownership is greater than 25 per cent and less than 75 per cent. The predominance of private ownership (more than 75 per cent) in water supply is indicated by 3.

criterion_notes.c1: The paper presents a broad comparative taxonomy of water utility management, privatization, pricing/cost-recovery policies, and agricultural irrigation water regimes. Although Section 3.2 narratively discusses residential piped water tariff affordability and network coverage using secondary sources, the study's empirical investigation (Section 3.4) examines national-level utility financial cost recovery rather than household or community water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 reading: (1) Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, this paper PASSES (yes) because it examines water utility ownership regimes (public vs. private share, concessions, leases, divestiture), tariff and subsidy policies, utility autonomy, irrigation property rights, and country-level governance, transparency/corruption, and political stability indicators. (2) Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type mechanism clarification, the paper FAILS (no) because its empirical model (Section 3.4) tests aggregate nationwide utility ownership share and unanalysed macro-governance background indices (World Bank governance, transparency, and stability) as determinants of utility financial cost recovery (CostRec), rather than a rule-type mechanism or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing household or community service access; meanwhile, the tariff and subsidy rules mentioned in Section 3.2 (increasing block rates, geographic targeting, means testing) are discussed only in a non-systematic narrative review without empirical testing. Because the empirical component also fails Criterion 4 (no service access or household affordability outcome), plain_criterion2_decision is still exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Sections 1-3.3 and 4 are a non-systematic narrative overview compiling secondary literature and descriptive tables (including reproducing Table 9 from Madhoo 2002), whereas Section 3.4 contains an original empirical cross-country econometric analysis (ordered logistic regression on 32 countries).
criterion_notes.c4: The sole dependent variable in the empirical analysis (Section 3.4) is CostRec, an ordinal 1-5 index measuring the extent to which water charges recover utility operation, maintenance, and capital costs of water production at the country level. This is a utility/sector financial cost-recovery outcome, not an outcome relevant to household or community access, connection, service availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: For the empirical investigation in Section 3.4, the unit of analysis and sample (32 countries: 16 developed and 16 developing), exposures (utility ownership, water availability, GNP per capita, GINI, foreign aid, and institutional indices), outcome (CostRec), and study design (cross-sectional cross-country ordered logistic regression) are clearly identifiable, though the outcome is outside review scope.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in English (with abstracts in English, French, German, and Spanish).

study_design: Cross-country cross-sectional econometric study (ordered logistic regression) combined with narrative literature review
country: Multi-country (32 countries in econometric sample: Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Cote D'Ivoire, India, Philippines, China, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, South Africa, Brazil, Thailand, Mexico, Malaysia, Chile, Mauritius, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Finland, Belgium, Netherlands, Sweden, Germany, Czech Republic, France, Japan, Canada, Denmark, Australia, Norway, UK, US)
population_and_sample: National piped water utility regimes across 32 countries (16 developing and 16 developed countries; unit of analysis: country)
exposure: Nationwide water utility ownership structure (public vs. private share), water resource availability, GNP per capita, income inequality (GINI), foreign aid (% of GDP), and World Bank institutional indices (governance, transparency/corruption, political stability)
outcome: National water utility cost recovery level (CostRec, ordinal 1-5 scale measuring recovery of O&M and capital costs of water production)
rationale: The retrieved full text matches the record metadata (Madhoo 2007, Annals of Public and Cooperative Economics). Most of the paper (Sections 1-3.3 and 4) is a non-systematic narrative taxonomy of public/private water utility regimes, residential and industrial water tariff structures, secondary literature on affordability, and agricultural irrigation water rights and pricing. Its sole original empirical component (Section 3.4) is a cross-country ordered logistic regression across 32 countries testing how nationwide utility ownership share, water availability, socioeconomic factors, and World Bank governance/transparency/stability indices affect national utility cost recovery (CostRec, scored 1-5 according to O&M and capital cost recovery). Because the empirical study measures only utility/sector financial cost recovery rather than household or community water/sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (and also relies on macro-level ownership share and macro-governance indices rather than a rule-type mechanism governing service access), the study is excluded as E04 (Wrong outcome). Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the decision remains exclude due to the lack of an eligible empirical access or affordability outcome.
